idiom_name: well-known symbol protocols (Symbol.iterator / Symbol.asyncIterator) + optional-property probing
implementation_notes: Capabilities are looked up by key, and ES2015 well-known symbols give those keys collision-free identity that the language itself treats as protocols: for...of and for await...of ask an object for Symbol.iterator / Symbol.asyncIterator (falling back to the sync iterator when the async one is absent), Array.from and spread ask for the iterator, and a library can register its own protocol with Symbol.for('acme.textAccessor'). The base interface is never touched - the consumer checks that obj[Symbol.asyncIterator] is a function and skips the value when it is not - and the extension can be supplied per object or per prototype without a class edit; an instanceof check against a small capability class is the idiomatic alternative for class-based extensions, while Proxy can synthesise arbitrary interfaces but costs a trap per access and loses identity.
pitfalls: Symbol-keyed members are invisible to Object.keys/for...in/JSON.stringify, so an extension set has to be documented - which is why MDN calls well-known symbols protocols rather than properties.
Symbol.for shares one global registry: two libraries can collide on the same key with no error and no versioning, so namespace the key.
Calling component[Symbol.iterator]() without a typeof guard throws TypeError: x is not iterable - a probe must test the member, not call it.

Mutating an object you do not own (or a shared prototype) is global state: defineProperty on prototypes is prototype pollution, and Proxy-wrapped interfaces break === and are far slower than plain property access.
